prompt: Which line correctly shows the algebraic derivation of the formula P = Fv for a constant force F acting on an object moving at constant velocity v in the direction of the force?
options: P = W / t, with W = Fs and v = s / t, so P = F(s / t) = Fv
P = W * t, with W = F / s and v = s * t, so P = Fv
P = F / t, with F = Ws and v = s / t, so P = Fv
P = Fs, with s = vt and W = Pt, so P = Fv / t

answer.explanation: Starting from the definition of power P = W / t, substituting work done W = Fs yields P = (Fs) / t = F(s / t). Since velocity v = s / t, this simplifies directly to P = Fv.

distractor_explanations: Option 1 is correct. It follows the syllabus derivation step-by-step.
Option 2 uses incorrect dimensional formulas: P = W * t is false.
Option 3 incorrectly claims P = F / t and F = Ws.
Option 4 confuses work with power and produces an invalid expression.
hints: Start with the definition of power: P = W / t.
Substitute W = Fs and recognize that s / t is velocity.
solution: P = W / t. Since W = Fs, P = F(s / t). For constant velocity, v = s / t, giving P = Fv. Option A is correct.
teacher_walkthrough: Define power as rate of work done: P = W / t.
Use work done by a constant force: W = Fs.
Substitute: P = (Fs) / t = F(s / t) = Fv.
